## Why all of this sounds artificial

By now this probably sounds terribly artificial. Is anyone actually going to do scheduled check-ins, delayed cohabitation, conversations about hypothetical disasters, imagination exercises, not to mention resisting the heat of the moment stuff, and continuing your own reparenting practices when a warm body is available to do some of the soothing?

Well, you caught me. It is painfully artificial. In a healthy communal society, the couple would have access to witnesses, elders, friends, and other emotional outlets and resources. Most of us these days don’t have that, so we’re trying to recreate consciously and clumsily some of what the wider field would have done without a checklist. You might even suspect that I'm subtly trying to influence you into wanting to forget all this and just join a community! And I couldn't even say you're wrong.

---

## What doing it consciously looks like

Some of these lessons came through thought. Most arrived through failure. A few are still being tested.

- Have the big conversations before making love. Talk while you can still hear each other clearly about jealousy, attraction to other people, stress behavior, old patterns, how recent the healing is, what each person wants in a hard moment, and money. Use scenarios: When X happens, I would want Y and probably do Z. Abstract answers usually mean there is no answer yet.
- Don’t let everything speed up at once. Resist early cohabitation, and set real check-in dates before there’s a crisis. Housing may make separate living difficult, but once you live together, practical necessity starts narrowing your choices.
- Make deep friends together, and remember that old friends will naturally be partial. The goal is to have some friends who know both of you as a couple instead of arriving only as defenders of one person’s story.
- Separate the romantic decision from the long-term decision. Somebody may be a wonderful lover and a terrible co-parent, community member, or life partner. Also notice when “I’m taking a chance on this person” quietly becomes “this is the right person.” The first answer may come quickly. The second needs more time.
- Keep your inner practices. Don’t let being loved become the reason you stop learning to love and regulate yourself.
- Pace the heavy conversations. Ten profound talks in one weekend can feel deep before the relationship has roots. Let play and ordinary time sit between them. Some information is better observed than extracted.
- Let discomfort remain information. Wait. I want to slow down. Something doesn’t fit. I need to ask this. Don’t let early chemistry automatically overrule that part of you.

---

# If you’re already in it

Most of this article is about what to do before the relationship gets its own momentum. If you’re already married, raising children, living together, or ten years in, advice about slowing down arrives a little late.

I wish I had a special method for fixing that. Mostly I learned the obvious thing the hard way: one person can’t create mutual honesty.

I learned that in all three of my reference relationships. Actually, it’s probably just common sense. I could keep bringing up the same problem, but I couldn’t make the other person look at it with me.

With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust. They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else. It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none.
